clinicalPearls: The rarest classical CDA and the only one classically autosomal dominant; the familial form is caused by a heterozygous KIF23 variant.
The bone marrow shows giant multinucleated erythroblasts ('gigantoblasts') containing many nuclei.
KIF23 encodes the mitotic kinesin MKLP1, essential for cytokinesis, so nuclear division in erythroblasts fails to complete.
Anaemia is typically mild with only modest haemolysis, and iron overload is less prominent than in CDA types I or II.
Long-term associations include monoclonal gammopathy and multiple myeloma, warranting periodic surveillance.
Retinal angioid streaks and a macular dystrophy may develop and threaten vision.
Both a well-characterised dominant familial form and sporadic cases are recognised.
reference.pathophysiology: The familial dominant form of CDA type III is caused by a heterozygous variant in KIF23, which encodes mitotic kinesin-like protein 1 (MKLP1), a component of the centralspindlin complex required for central-spindle assembly and completion of cytokinesis. Impaired cytokinesis in the erythroid lineage yields the characteristic very large, multinucleated erythroblasts (gigantoblasts) and ineffective erythropoiesis; unlike CDA types I and II, haemolysis and pathological iron loading are comparatively mild, which shapes both the milder anaemia and the distinct complication profile.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count, reticulocyte count and blood film
Bone marrow examination for giant multinucleated erythroblasts
Serum protein electrophoresis with immunoglobulins and free light chains for paraproteinaemia
Ophthalmological assessment for angioid streaks and maculopathy
redFlags: Emergence of a monoclonal paraprotein or overt myeloma
Visual disturbance from angioid streaks or macular degeneration
reference.prognosis: Generally a mild disorder compatible with a normal or near-normal lifespan; the principal concerns are surveillance for monoclonal gammopathy and myeloma and for sight-threatening retinopathy.
pitfalls: Giant multinucleated erythroblasts can be mistaken for myelodysplasia or erythroleukaemia.
The dominant inheritance means an affected parent is usually identifiable in the pedigree.
Monitoring for paraproteinaemia and retinopathy should be ongoing rather than a single baseline assessment.
Its milder haemolysis and iron loading can lead to underestimation compared with CDA types I and II.
